title: In re Debs (1895)
summary: The national government may go to a federal court of equity for an injunction against obstructions of interstate commerce and the mails without a statute expressly authorizing the suit, and may punish disobedience as contempt.
notes:
Key line: The strong arm of the national government may be put forth to brush away all obstructions to the freedom of interstate commerce or the transportation of the mails. (Justice Brewer)

Citation: 158 U.S. 564 (1895).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Eugene V. Debs, president of the American Railway Union, and other officers of the union, George W. Howard, Sylvester Keliher and L. W. Rogers, who were imprisoned for contempt of an injunction issued during the Pullman strike of 1894. The respondent was the United States, which had filed the bill in equity under the direction of Attorney General Richard Olney through Thomas E. Milchrist, district attorney for the Northern District of Illinois. Clarence Darrow and Lyman Trumbull argued for the petitioners; Attorney General Olney and Edwin Walker argued for the Government. The proceeding was an original petition for habeas corpus in the Supreme Court.
sections.Material Facts: In May 1894 a dispute between the Pullman Palace Car Company and its employees led many of them to leave its service. Officers of the American Railway Union, to force a settlement, organized a boycott of Pullman cars, directing members not to handle trains carrying them and calling strikes on railroads that did. The boycott spread to twenty-two railroads entering Chicago, which carried more than twelve million passengers a year and the mails, and traffic was obstructed by strikes, threats and violence. On July 2, 1894, the United States filed a bill in the Circuit Court for the Northern District of Illinois alleging an unlawful conspiracy to obstruct interstate commerce and the mails and seeking an injunction. The court issued the injunction that day, forbidding the defendants from interfering with the railroads' business, the mails and interstate commerce and from inducing employees to quit by threats or violence. The defendants continued to direct the strike in disobedience of the order.
sections.Procedural History: The Government moved to have the defendants attached for contempt. After a hearing, on December 14, 1894, the Circuit Court, Judge Woods presiding, found Debs and his associates guilty of contempt and sentenced them to jail terms of three to six months, 64 Fed. 724. Having been committed, they applied to the Supreme Court on January 14, 1895, for a writ of error and a writ of habeas corpus. The writ of error was denied on January 17 because the contempt order was not a final judgment, but the Court entertained the habeas petition. It was argued on March 25 and 26, 1895, and decided on May 27, 1895. The petition was denied. Justice Brewer wrote for a unanimous Court.
sections.Issue: Did the Circuit Court have jurisdiction to entertain a bill in equity filed by the United States and to issue an injunction against the officers of the railway union, so that its contempt order was valid and habeas corpus must be denied? Two questions were involved. First, are the relations of the general government to interstate commerce and the transportation of the mails such that it may intervene to remove obstructions to them? Second, if so, may the government seek relief in a court of equity by injunction, without a statute expressly authorizing such a suit and despite the fact that the obstructions were also crimes, or is it limited to the use of executive force and criminal prosecution?
sections.Holding: Yes on both questions, and the petition is denied. The United States has full sovereignty within the sphere of its enumerated powers, including power over interstate commerce and the mails, and those powers have been put into exercise by legislation. The national government may remove everything placed on highways, natural or artificial, that obstructs interstate commerce or the carriage of the mails, using the whole executive power if necessary. It is equally within its competence to appeal to the civil courts to determine whether obstructions exist and to invoke the powers of equity to remove or restrain them. That jurisdiction is not defeated because the obstructions are also crimes or because the remedy is enforced by contempt. The bill showed an existing and threatened obstruction, the court had power to issue the injunction, and its contempt findings are not reviewable on habeas corpus.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Brewer described the case as one in which the United States, finding interstate transportation and the mails through Chicago obstructed by a combination of thousands, chose the civil courts rather than the army. He affirmed that the national government is not a mere confederation; it acts directly on every citizen, and within its enumerated powers it has the full attributes of sovereignty. If a single State's inhabitants could paralyze interstate commerce with the government limited to prosecuting individuals afterward, the Nation would be at their mercy. There is no such impotency: the strong arm of the national government may be put forth to brush away all obstructions to the freedom of interstate commerce or the transportation of the mails. But a government that can use force may also prefer the courts, and it is in the interest of peace and order that it do so. Equity has long enjoined public nuisances obstructing highways at the suit of the sovereign, and railroads are the highways of interstate commerce. The government need not show a property interest; it may sue to protect the public rights it is charged with securing. That the acts were also crimes did not oust equity, since the injunction protects civil rights and a contempt penalty is no bar to prosecution. Brewer declined to rest on the Sherman Act, preferring the broader ground so that the principles would be fully stated.
